title: Whisky for Procurement Teams | Craft Beer School
desc: What a whisky buyer actually buys: grain, molasses spirit, malt, casks, glass and closures, plus the specs that decide quality.
teaser: A whisky buyer signs off on spirit, oak and glass. Each one has a spec that the blender cares about more than the price.
standfirst: Procurement in a whisky company is not office supplies with a higher unit cost. The spirit, the casks and the bottle all shape what ends up in the glass. Here is what each line on your purchase register does on the production floor.
sections: Most of what you buy ends up in the bottle

A bottle of whisky is mostly two things: spirit and water. Around it sit a cask that flavoured the spirit, a glass bottle, a closure, a label and a carton. A procurement team buys almost all of these. That makes the buyer one of the few people outside production whose choices a drinker can taste.

In India the spirit side splits two ways. Much of what the domestic market calls whisky is a blend of neutral spirit with some malt or grain whisky for character. Indian single malts and premium blends rely on malted barley distilled in copper pot stills and then aged in oak. Our guide to the Indian whisky market explains why both exist on the same shelf. For a buyer the point is simple: the two need very different specifications.
Neutral spirit is bought on a certificate

Extra neutral alcohol (ENA) is spirit distilled in columns to a very high strength, usually above 95% ABV, so that it carries little flavour of its own. In India it is made mainly from sugarcane molasses or from grain such as broken rice and maize. Each tanker arrives with a certificate of analysis.

The numbers on that certificate are what the blender reads first: strength, methanol, aldehydes, esters, higher alcohols and residue on evaporation. A cheaper ENA with higher aldehydes can push a harsh, green apple edge into the final blend. When a buyer switches supplier to save a few rupees a litre, the quality lab should taste a sample before the first full tanker is booked. Grain ENA and molasses ENA also taste different, which is why many blends specify one.
Malt and grain carry their own specs

For a malt distillery, malted barley is the biggest raw material. Maltsters quote moisture (usually around 4 to 5%) and extract. For peated malt they also quote phenol content in parts per million. Distillers also care about predicted spirit yield: how many litres of pure alcohol a tonne of malt should give. A batch with low extract gives less spirit per rupee even when its price per tonne looked better.

Indian distillers use both imported two-row barley malt and malt made from Indian six-row barley. Grain distilleries buy maize, broken rice or millet by moisture and starch. A wet lot of maize in the monsoon can heat and grow mould in storage before it ever reaches the cooker.
Casks are the slowest purchase you will make

Whisky gets most of its colour and much of its flavour from oak. Scotch must mature for at least three years in oak casks. Most Indian malt is aged in American oak barrels that once held bourbon, because bourbon law requires new charred oak containers and so used barrels come onto the market. Sherry butts, wine casks and new oak appear for finishes.

A standard American barrel holds around 200 litres. Casks are bought years before the whisky they will hold is sold, often from overseas, with long shipping times and import paperwork. A buyer who sources casks well has to think in maturation cycles, not quarters. In Indian heat whisky ages faster and evaporation runs higher than in Scotland, so cask size and type matter even more.
Dry goods cause most of the stock-outs

The liquid is rarely what stops a bottling line. Glass, closures, labels and cartons do. Bottles in India come in standard sizes such as 750 ml, 375 ml and 180 ml. Each state may need its own label, which multiplies label SKUs quickly.

  • Glass needs a tolerance on fill height and neck finish, or the capper jams.
  • Closures need a matching spec for the neck and the pilfer-proof band.
  • Labels must carry state-specific declarations, so a wrong print run cannot be reused elsewhere.

When a festive season approaches, the line usually waits on a label approval or a glass delivery, not on whisky.

A specification is only useful if both buyer and supplier agree what happens when a delivery misses it. For spirit, that means a sample tested on arrival before the tanker unloads into a storage tank. Once ENA is pumped into a vat holding 50,000 litres of good spirit, a bad load cannot be separated out again.

For casks, the agreement covers wood type, previous fill, char or toast level, how long since the cask was emptied and whether it arrives whole or knocked down into staves. A cask that dried out in transit leaks when filled. For glass, it covers weight, dimensions and defect limits. Buyers who write these down with the quality lab before the contract is signed avoid most of the arguments that follow a rejected load. The lab should also keep a retained sample of each delivery for at least as long as the product it went into is on sale.
What your team gains from tasting the product

Buyers who have never nosed new make spirit next to a five year old whisky negotiate on price alone. A short, guided session changes that. When a procurement analyst smells the difference between ENA from two suppliers, the specification starts to make sense. When they see a cask opened and the colour of the spirit inside, a cask invoice stops being an abstract line item.

Tastings at work should always be opt-in, within company policy, with spit cups and water on the table. Non-drinkers learn just as much from nosing. Our beginner's whisky tasting guide covers the basics.

A good first step: ask your quality lab for last month's certificates of analysis for your top three suppliers and sit with a blender for an hour to read them together.
faqs: Do procurement teams need to know how whisky is made?
Enough to read a specification. Knowing why methanol, aldehydes or cask type matter helps a buyer judge when a cheaper option will change the product.
Why are casks so hard to buy?
Most are imported used barrels with long lead times. They are bought years before the whisky inside them is sold, so planning runs on maturation cycles.
No. Molasses and grain ENA taste different. Batches vary in aldehydes, esters and higher alcohols, which is why every tanker comes with a certificate of analysis.
